01

Reference assets

These two images are the style. Every colour, texture and depth rule below is taken from them, and every new image should be generated with one of them attached as a style reference. They set the look, not the subject: a new image keeps the paper, depth and palette but depicts whatever the piece is about.

A · Single arch
One cut edge. The scene spills out at the lower left. Use for most pieces.
reference-a.jpg
B · Stepped arch
Two concentric cut edges — a deco step — with the scene aligned to the arch's right edge. Use for title pieces and covers.
reference-b.jpg

Anatomy — what makes it work

1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8
  1. Recessed window. The arch is cut into the front sheet; its edge throws a soft shadow onto the scene at top and left.
  2. Shallow relief with shadow lines. Every shape casts a narrow shadow on the one behind — a few millimetres of depth, not a diorama.
  3. Light against dark. Adjacent layers alternate in tone (pale path against dark hedge, cream tower against olive block) so every edge reads.
  4. Spill-out. The lower-left of the scene — trunk, ground, bench — breaks out of the arch onto the page, ending in a soft wavy cut.
  5. Plants grow from the scene. The tree is rooted inside the picture and its canopy crosses the arch edge; leaves sit both in front of and behind other layers.
  6. Simple folded leaves. Almond shapes with a single central fold — one lit half, one shaded half — and no vein detail. A few drift outside as the motif.
  7. One accent mass. A single crimson disc dominates; crimson is then echoed only in small pieces (some leaves, one figure). Accent covers about 2% of the image.
  8. Scale contrast. Tiny figures and buildings against a large tree and bench give depth without detail.
02

Principles

Layered

Depth from stacked matte card and narrow shadows. Never gradients, gloss or 3D rendering.

Quiet

Muted greens, sands and linen. One accent, one dominant accent shape.

Spacious

At least a third of any composition is plain paper.

Framed & freed

Imagery sits in an arch but always escapes it somewhere, so it belongs to the page.

Deco type

Thin geometric capitals, wide tracking, fine double rules — elegance, not ornament.

Accent rules: one accent per piece or set · one dominant accent shape (sun, disc, doorway) plus small echoes · about 2–5% of the image · never lightened into pinks or tints.

Proportion (as in reference A)

Roughly: paper and lights 65–75%, greens and darks 20–30%, accent 2–5%.

Contrast ratios to WCAG 2.1: 4.5 : 1 minimum for body text, 3 : 1 for large headings. Poiret One's hairline strokes look lighter than the ratio suggests, so give it more contrast, not less.

05

Motifs & ornaments

Motifs come from the image

A motif is a single small element lifted from the main illustration's own subject, in the same paper style — never a fixed ornament. In the references it is a folded leaf; for a coastal piece it might be a shell, for a workshop a wood shaving. Crop it from the generated image, or generate it separately on plain paper with the reference attached.

Count: one to three per piece. Size: 4–8% of the short edge. Place: a corner, beside a label, or drifting off the illustration (as the falling leaves do). Colour: whatever the subject has; the accent version only if the accent isn't already crowded.

Examples above are cropped from reference A.

Deco ornaments — built in code

Double rule
1.5 px over 0.75 px. Separates title from label.
Diamond divider
Between blocks on type-only pieces. Max one per piece.
Stepped corners
Frames a text block on a coloured ground.
Stepped arch line
Echo of reference B for type-only pieces.

Ornaments are hairline, in ink, olive or linen — never the accent, never filled, never more than two kinds in one piece.

Sequences

In a carousel or series: one accent throughout; grounds move light → dark → light (paper, forest or olive, sand, crimson, paper); no two dark grounds side by side; at most two generated images per set.

07

Imagery workflow

Testing showed that text prompts alone never reached this look; attaching a reference image did so in one step. So every new image is made with reference A or B attached and a short prompt that names only the new subject.

Using the attached image as the style reference, create a new image in exactly
the same handmade paper-cut style, palette, paper texture, lighting and shallow
depth. Keep the same arch window cut into cream paper [single arch | stepped
double arch], with the scene spilling out of the lower left of the arch onto the
page, and a plant or tree growing from inside the scene across the arch edge.

New subject: [SUBJECT — e.g. a quiet harbour with moored boats and a lighthouse].

Keep: one deep crimson disc as the only large accent shape, with crimson echoed
only in two or three small pieces. Leaves are simple folded almond shapes. Tiny
figures or buildings in the distance for scale. Square format, arch centred
slightly right, generous plain paper to the left. No text, letters or numbers.

Check every result against

  • The eight anatomy points in section 01.
  • Palette: nothing outside the swatches; no pinks or tints of the accent.
  • Accent: one dominant shape, small echoes only, about 2–5% of the image.
  • Relief stays shallow — no pop-up platforms or triple frames.
  • No text, signatures or stray symbols.

Known weaknesses to watch

  • Generators repeat objects (reference A has two near-identical benches).
  • Accent tends to multiply — scattered crimson leaves creep upwards.
  • Detailed subjects (tools, machines) simplify poorly; prefer settings and silhouettes.
  • Free-tier images are about 1024 px square: enough for social, marginal for large print.
08

Do & don't

Do
  • Attach a reference image to every generation.
  • Set all type and ornaments in code; generate images without text.
  • Leave a third or more as plain paper; left-align text by default.
  • Use Poiret One only large; Josefin Sans for everything small.
  • Derive motifs from the image's own subject.
Don't
  • Mix crimson and terracotta in one piece or set.
  • Tint the accent, or set text on khaki or sage.
  • Use bold weights, text shadows or more than two ornament types.
  • Box the scene fully inside the arch — it must escape somewhere.
  • Mix illustration styles (photos, line art, 3D) in one piece or set.
